To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
deep learning models trained and tested on Landsat 7 and Landsat 8 show high cloud detection accuracy when trained on one dataset and tested on a different dataset of the same satellite.

(i) deep learning models trained and tested on different Landsat datasets and Sentinel 2 datasets exhibit similar performance as operational threshold based algorithms; (ii) deep learning models exhibit high performance in intra dataset validation, i.e. when trained and tested in the same Landsat dataset; and (iii) the development of new deep learning models for cloud detection in Landsat 9 images can be based on models trained on Landsats 7, 8 and 9 datasets.

(i) deep learning models outperform operational algorithms when tested on independent images of the same dataset, (ii) deep learning models trained and tested on Landsat 7 data perform similarly to those trained and tested on other Landsat 8 datasets, and (iii) deep learning models perform comparably to operational algorithms when they are trained and tested on Sentinel 2 data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of deep learning models for cloud detection in Landsat 7 and 8 images.
the benchmarking of deep learning models for cloud detection in optical satellite images.
the benchmarking of cloud detection models in satellite imagery and the comparison of deep learning models with threshold based methods.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

deep learning models can outperform the operational cloud detection methods when they are trained and tested using the same dataset, but the performance is similar to the operational ones when tested on different datasets.
deep learning models outperform the operational algorithms in the Landsat 8 domain, and the performance is similar when tested on Sentinel 2 data.

, in the absence of a standard benchmark, deep learning models trained in the same conditions outperform the operational algorithms in terms of cloud detection, while the comparison between different deep learning models is not clear.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of deep learning models for cloud detection in optical satellite images has a strong dependence on the dataset used to train and test them.
the deep learning model is not a universal solution for cloud detection, and the results are highly dependent on the dataset used.

the deep learning models are better than the traditional threshold based algorithms for cloud detection in intra dataset validation but they are not better than the traditional algorithms in inter dataset validation or cross sensor validation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the development of deep learning based cloud detection algorithms is not yet a solved problem.

, although deep learning models can outperform threshold-based approaches in some cases, they are not a panacea for cloud detection, and their performance is highly dataset dependent, especially for thin clouds.

the performance of deep neural networks in cloud detection can be improved by training the network with a dataset that contains the same types of clouds as those that will be encountered during inference, and by using the best available data from the same satellite sensor.
